newsitem.title: CANADA: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE SET FOR EMOTIONAL HOME CONTEST.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE SET FOR EMOTIONAL HOME CONTEST.

text.p: Jacques Villeneuve faces one of the most emotionally charged contests of his racing career this weekend when he attempts to emulate his father Gilles' 1978 triumph and deliver Williams' 100th victory in his home Canadian Grand Prix.

Villeneuve, 26, who was forced to fly to Paris on Wednesday to be reprimanded by the sport's ruling body, the Federation International de l'Automobile (FIA), admitted he had strong and special feelings about Sunday's race, on Fathers' Day, on the circuit named after his father.

Before facing the FIA's world council to explain the undignified tone of his remarks in criticism of the controversial 1998 technical regulations, Villeneuve said: "This is the most important race of the season to me personally.
"It's very special. Last year, I had a good race, but didn't win. This time, I really want to go one better if I can."

After his commanding victory in last month's Spanish Grand Prix at Barcelona, Villeneuve is back atop the drivers' championship with 30 points to German Michael Schumacher's 27 and hopes he can extend that lead and put Williams back in charge of the constructors' title chase at the same time by toppling Ferrari.
The low-grip track on the Ile Notre Dame in the St Laurence river is hard on brakes, fuel and cars. Last year, there were only eight classified finishers
Two of them were Williams, the Canadian following home world champion Damon Hill.

"The fans are amazing," said Villeneuve, looking ahead to the race before his Paris reprimand which also upset his bid to acclimatise to the heat and time difference in Montreal. "They are respectful and it feels great to race there -- mostly because it is my home crowd.

"But it feels great for me to go there as leader. I felt under a lot of pressure in Barcelona so it was good to win and get back in front before Montreal because there is going to be enough pressure around that race as it is.

"The track is not really anything special, in qualifying, because there are no high-speed corners, so you don't get a big rush out of it. But it is very good for racing because you have a lot of overtaking areas and braking zones."
Apart from the jet-lag problem after his return from France, Villeneuve also faces a strong threat from team-mate Heinz-Harald Frentzen.

"We have been very competitive at all the other tracks this year so I am confident it will be the same in Montreal," Frentzen said. "I know Jacques will be very motivated to win at home, but I can assure you I will not be doing him any favours."
A victory be either Williams driver would be their 100th since entering Formula One in 1978, in 306 outings, a strike record untouched by any other team.

The biggest challenge to Williams should come from Ferrari, again, but both the Benetton and McLaren teams should do well. Benetton dominated last week's test at the Magny-Cours circuit in France with Frenchman Jean Alesi topping the times and they will run their cars with revised aerodynamic and chassis arrangements.

"We have made some progress and we feel confident of doing better," said technical director Pat Symonds. "It is just a matter of adding a little luck to the equation and I think we could be in for a better run of results."

For Ferrari, Schumacher said: "I have to admit we are a lot better placed at this stage of the season than I thought we were going to be. I was happy to come away with three points after the Spanish Grand Prix.

"In Montreal, we should be in much better shape and if our excellent reliability continues, I am sure we can stay in strong contention for the title even if we do not have the quickest outright package at the moment."
